meta.note: Computational and literature summary only. No discovery claims; not medical advice.
meta.overlooked_rule: Solid evidence (Mendelian database link for neurological diseases, or exome/structural-variant association) and at most 60 PubMed title/abstract records for the official symbol, symbol not ambiguous. A flag is a starting point: each still needs a check for focused mechanistic papers, competition and feasibility. Flags removed after manual checks are marked.

mpfc.name: Medial prefrontal cortex
mpfc.does: Front, inner surface of the frontal lobe. Involved in thinking about oneself, other people and decisions.
mpfc.self: Part of the cortical midline structures that light up whenever people judge things in relation to themselves. A meta-analysis splits it into a ventral part (tagging information as 'about me') and a dorsal part (evaluating it).

acc.name: Anterior cingulate cortex
acc.does: A belt of cortex above the corpus callosum that monitors conflict and errors and links emotion to action.
acc.self: In a small PET study, people with schizophrenia who felt their movements were controlled from outside showed over-activity here and in parietal cortex; it settled as the symptom improved.

pcc.name: Posterior cingulate & precuneus
pcc.does: Inner back surface of the brain; a hub of the brain's resting 'default mode' network.
pcc.self: The posterior part of the cortical midline structures, active during self-related processing across tasks.

thal.name: Thalamus
thal.does: Central relay that passes sensory and motor signals to the cortex.
thal.self: Cortical midline structures are densely linked with subcortical midline regions; the meta-analysis argues for one cortical-subcortical midline system for the self.

hippo.name: Hippocampus & entorhinal cortex
hippo.does: Inner temporal lobe; essential for forming new memories.
hippo.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here.

sn.name: Substantia nigra & striatum
sn.does: Dopamine-making neurons in the midbrain (substantia nigra) that signal to the striatum to start and smooth movement.
sn.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here. Dopamine's role in the comparator model of delusions of control is named as an open question.

cereb.name: Cerebellum
cereb.does: Back of the brain under the cortex; fine-tunes movement by predicting its outcome.
cereb.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here.

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.does: Connects brain and spinal cord; controls breathing, eye movements and arousal.
brainstem.self: An eye-movement pathway from the brainstem to the frontal cortex is the best-worked-out example of a corollary discharge, the brain's internal copy of its own movement commands; this signal appears disrupted in schizophrenia.

pfc.name: Lateral prefrontal cortex
pfc.does: Outer front of the brain; planning, working memory and control of attention.
pfc.self: Rare damaging variants in schizophrenia are most enriched in genes specific to frontal cortex (SCHEMA). Frontal brain stimulation improved action-outcome monitoring in a schizophrenia study.

motor.name: Motor & premotor cortex
motor.does: Strip in front of the central sulcus that plans and sends movement commands.
motor.self: Every movement command is sent out with a copy (corollary discharge) that lets the brain predict what it will feel. If the prediction fails, one's own actions can feel caused by someone else: the comparator model of delusions of control.

parietal.name: Inferior parietal cortex / temporo-parietal junction
parietal.does: Outer back-middle of the brain; combines body position, attention and the sense of who caused an action.
parietal.self: In patients with passivity experiences (feeling controlled from outside), this area was over-active during voluntary movement and calmed as symptoms improved (small PET study, 7 patients). Parietal cortex is a recurring candidate in self-monitoring models.

auditory.name: Auditory cortex (temporal lobe)
auditory.does: Upper temporal lobe; processes sound and speech.
auditory.self: Before we speak, motor areas warn the auditory cortex to expect our own voice. Failure of this warning is a leading explanation for why inner speech can be heard as an outside voice.

insula.name: Insula
insula.does: Cortex folded deep inside the lateral sulcus; senses the body's inner state.
insula.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here, although it is often discussed in bodily-self research.

self_story.t: Self-disorders (from the German Ichstörungen) are changes in the first-person sense of being oneself: thoughts that feel inserted, actions that feel controlled from outside, a self that feels thin or unreal. They have long been tied to schizophrenia, especially early on.

self_story.h: How strong is the evidence that they mark schizophrenia?
self_story.t: Across 25 studies (690 patients), people with schizophrenia showed clear disturbances of the minimal self (overall effect size 0.51; sense of agency 0.49). An updated 2026 meta-analysis of 38 studies found self-disorder scores highest in the schizophrenia spectrum, intermediate in people at clinical high risk, and lower in other mental disorders. Body ownership, by contrast, was not impaired in a dedicated experiment plus meta-analysis. Agency findings also depend on the task: some studies show too little self-attribution, others too much.

self_story.h: Is there a 'centre of the I' in the brain?
self_story.t: No single centre has been found. Two systems keep coming up. (1) Cortical midline structures (medial prefrontal, anterior and posterior cingulate, precuneus) are active whenever we process information about ourselves. (2) A prediction system: each action is sent out with an internal copy (corollary discharge) so the brain can recognise the result as self-made. When this fails, one's own thoughts, speech or movements can feel foreign. Taking a first-person perspective engages medial prefrontal, medial parietal and lateral temporoparietal cortex.

Patients whose own hand acts against their will (alien limb, 50 lesion cases) had lesions in many places, but all fell within one network connected to the precuneus; lesions removing the will to act (akinetic mutism, 28 cases) mapped to a network connected to the anterior cingulate. A 2026 case analysis with systematic review of post-stroke alien hand found that the sense of agency was always disrupted, while the sense of owning the limb was lost mainly with parietal lesions.

self_story.h: Which areas look different in people with these experiences?
self_story.t: Evidence is small but specific. In a PET study, patients who felt their movements were controlled from outside over-activated parietal and cingulate cortex, and this reversed as the symptom faded. Corollary discharge deficits have been measured in speech-to-hearing and eye-movement pathways.

self_story.h: Which genes and proteins are involved?
self_story.t: No gene has been linked specifically to self-disorders: we found no study tying a risk gene to these experiences. The closest genetic bridge: people with a 22q11.2 deletion, a high-risk genetic form of schizophrenia, showed clear deficits in monitoring their own actions and over-attributed actions to themselves in virtual-reality tests, before any psychosis. This links a risk deletion to a sense-of-agency measure, not to a single gene. What is known is for schizophrenia as a whole: 287 common-variant loci concentrated in neuron-expressed genes, 10 genes with rare damaging variants of large effect (including the glutamate receptors GRIN2A and GRIA3), enrichment in frontal-cortex-specific genes, and complement C4A, which tags synapses for removal. Linking these genes to the self-network regions is an open analysis, listed as a NeuroUnknown next step.

self_story.h: Do current treatments target the cause?
self_story.t: No. All long-established antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors; they reduce psychosis but do not repair the underlying biology. Only about 1 in 7 people meet strict recovery criteria (median 13.5% across 50 studies), and this has not improved over decades. The first approved drug without direct D2 blockade, xanomeline-trospium (a muscarinic M1/M4 agonist), reduced symptoms in phase 3, but it also treats symptoms. A glycine-transporter drug for the glutamate hypothesis (iclepertin) failed to improve cognition in three phase 3 trials.

Not today. Many people improve and some recover, but no treatment removes the cause, because the cause is spread over hundreds of genes and developmental factors. Neurology shows what a cure-like treatment can look like when one gene is the cause: in spinal muscular atrophy, an RNA drug that corrects the faulty gene's product let 51% of treated infants reach motor milestones versus 0% without it. Schizophrenia has no single causal gene of that kind, but rare large-effect genes such as GRIN2A are the closest starting points.

self_story.h: An experimental lead on the self itself
self_story.t: A small study found that frontal transcranial direct current stimulation improved action-outcome monitoring in schizophrenia spectrum disorder, the process thought to fail in passivity experiences. This is a proof of concept, not a treatment.

diseases.name: Schizophrenia & psychosis
diseases.intro: Schizophrenia is a disorder in which perception, thinking and the sense of being oneself can change, usually beginning in late adolescence or early adulthood. It is highly heritable, but the risk is spread over hundreds of genetic variants that mostly act in neurons and synapses, together with environmental factors. Psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions are linked to disturbed signalling in dopamine and glutamate circuits; current medicines act on these signals rather than on the underlying causes.
causes: Heritability is estimated at 60-80%; 287 common-variant loci act mainly through genes expressed in excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
Rare damaging variants in 10 genes raise risk 3- to 50-fold, including the glutamate receptor subunits GRIN2A and GRIA3.
A 2026 preprint (not yet peer reviewed) of 87,959 cases reports 16 exome-wide genes, including XPO7, SCAF1, FYN and SCN2A.
Higher C4A complement activity raises risk; in mice C4 drives removal of synapses during development.

Of 170 environmental and developmental factors studied in 683 studies, only the ultra-high-risk clinical state and Black-Caribbean ethnicity in England had convincing evidence; urbanicity, migration, childhood trauma and childhood social withdrawal had weaker (suggestive) evidence.

guidelines: WFSBP guideline: acute treatment and treatment resistance (2012)
treat: Dopamine D2 receptors (blockade or partial agonism)
Reduces psychosis; median strict recovery only 13.5% across 50 studies.
The standard option when two other antipsychotics have failed (treatment resistance).
First approved drug without direct D2 blockade; PANSS -9.6 vs placebo at 5 weeks.
Small effect in a dose-response meta-analysis of 3 trials (SMD -0.23).
No improvement in cognition in three phase 3 trials.
diseases.cure: Not curable today. Treatments manage symptoms; strict recovery in about 1 in 7.

diseases.name: Bipolar disorder
diseases.intro: Bipolar disorder causes recurring episodes of mania or hypomania and depression, separated by periods of more stable mood. It is strongly genetic: dozens of risk loci point to synaptic signalling and neuron-specific genes. Long-term treatment aims to prevent new episodes.
causes: 64 genomic loci in 41,917 cases; risk alleles enriched in synaptic signalling and brain-expressed, neuron-specific genes.
Exome sequencing of 13,933 patients identified AKAP11 as a risk gene shared with schizophrenia.
related: shares AKAP11 and part of the genetic risk
treat: First-line for mania and maintenance (CANMAT/ISBD); fewer suicides than placebo (odds ratio 0.13).
Listed among first-line options for acute mania, bipolar depression or maintenance.
diseases.cure: Not curable today; long-term treatment prevents episodes in many people.

diseases.name: Major depression
diseases.intro: Major depression is a common illness of persistent low mood, loss of interest and changes in sleep, energy and thinking. Genetic risk is spread over hundreds of loci that point to synapses and specific neuron types. Treatment combines psychological, medication, lifestyle and brain-stimulation options chosen together with the patient.
causes: 697 associations at 635 loci in 688,808 cases from 29 countries; 308 high-confidence genes; postsynaptic density enriched.
guidelines: CANMAT 2023 update for major depressive disorder in adults
treat: Psychological, pharmacological, lifestyle, digital and neuromodulation treatments
CANMAT 2023 organises these by lines of treatment with shared decision-making.

diseases.cure: Many episodes remit; no treatment targets the underlying cause.

Rare variants in a few hundred genes, often active in early brain development, explain part of it; many more people carry common variants of small effect. diseases.name: Alzheimer's disease
diseases.intro: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. Amyloid-beta and tau proteins accumulate over many years, first damaging memory circuits in the hippocampus and later wider networks. Diagnosis increasingly uses biomarkers, and the first antibodies that remove amyloid slow decline modestly in early disease.
causes: 75 risk loci (42 new) in 111,326 clinically diagnosed or proxy cases.
Soluble and aggregated amyloid-beta may start or drive the disease process; lowering it slows decline modestly.
guidelines: European intersocietal recommendations for biomarker-based diagnosis (2024)
treat: CDR-SB decline slowed by 0.45 points over 18 months; ARIA and infusion reactions; for early AD with confirmed amyloid.
CDR-SB decline slowed by 0.67 points at 76 weeks (low/medium tau).
diseases.cure: Not curable. The first disease-modifying antibodies slow decline modestly in early disease.

diseases.name: Parkinson's disease
diseases.intro: Parkinson's disease is a progressive disorder in which dopamine-producing neurons of the substantia nigra are lost and the protein alpha-synuclein aggregates in nerve cells. It causes slowness, rigidity and tremor, and many non-motor symptoms. Dopamine replacement works well for movement symptoms but does not stop the disease.
causes: 90 independent risk signals in 37,688 cases; risk loci are brain-enriched and point to specific neuron types.
Aggregated alpha-synuclein is central to the disease process and can be detected with seed amplification assays.
guidelines: AAN practice guideline: dopaminergic therapy for early Parkinson disease (2021)
treat: Greater motor benefit than dopamine agonists as initial therapy, with more dyskinesia (AAN 2021).
Less motor benefit and less dyskinesia than levodopa as initial therapy.
Missed its phase 2 primary endpoint; exploratory slower motor progression in fast progressors.
diseases.cure: Not curable; no approved treatment slows the disease.

diseases.name: ALS (motor neuron disease)
diseases.intro: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis destroys the motor neurons of the brain and spinal cord, causing progressive weakness. About one in 350 people develop it. Some cases are caused by single genes such as SOD1, which now allows gene-targeted treatment for that form.
causes: Lifetime risk about 1 in 350; 15 risk loci in 29,612 patients with distinct genetic architectures.
Mutations in SOD1 cause one inherited form; lowering SOD1 is a direct, cause-targeted strategy.
guidelines: EAN guideline on the management of ALS (2024)
treat: Multidisciplinary care, nutrition and ventilation support
Recommended in the EAN 2024 guideline alongside available disease-modifying treatments.
Lowered SOD1 and neurofilament; missed the 28-week primary endpoint; longer data favoured early start.
diseases.cure: Not curable. Gene-targeted silencing now exists for the SOD1 form.
